Article Title: In 1997, Martha Stewart bought Edsel Ford's 63-acre Maine estate for reportedly under $6 million; she restored its historic landscape while preserving the 12-bedroom stone house and Ford family china
Article Text:
In 1997, Martha Stewart bought Edsel Ford's 63-acre Maine estate for reportedly under $6 million (Image Credit: Architectural Digest)

A retreat created for Edsel Ford

She restored its historic landscape while preserving the 12-bedroom stone house and Ford family china (Image Credit: Architectural Digest)

Stewart preserved the house rather than remaking it

Interiors reflect both Ford history and Stewart’s style

Stewart has added her own design touches, but they have generally been incorporated alongside the property's existing character (Image Credit: Architectural Digest)

A landscape shaped by history

Perched above Seal Harbor on Maine’s Mount Desert Island, Skylands carries nearly a century of history tied to the Ford family and is now closely associated with Martha Stewart. Stewart bought the 63-acre estate in 1997, reportedly for just under $6 million, and has since treated the property as a piece of American architectural and landscape history rather than simply a summer home. In her own Martha Stewart Blog, she described the estate’s history and the work involved in bringing its Jens Jensen-designed landscape back towards its original character.Skylands was developed for Edsel Ford, the son of Henry Ford, and his wife, Eleanor. The house was completed in 1925 and designed by architect Duncan Candler, while renowned landscape designer Jens Jensen created the surrounding landscape. Architectural Digest describes the three-story stone residence as sitting high above Seal Harbor, with a setting shaped by granite outcrops, trees, ferns and terraces rather than a conventional manicured lawn.The estate's design was closely connected to its natural surroundings. Jensen incorporated elements including mossy woods, ferns, evergreens and maples into the landscape, creating a setting that blended the house with the terrain around it.In a 2013 post on her blog, Stewart wrote that the Ford estate had been sold to another family and said the property had not been maintained in the same way as it had been during the Fords’ ownership. When she purchased Skylands in 1997, she brought in landscape architect Patrick Chassé to help with the restoration of Jensen’s work. Stewart wrote that Chassé helped with the design of a council ring while also addressing the “challenges and compromises” involved in bringing the historic landscape back to its natural character.The character of Skylands has remained closely tied to its original architecture. Architectural Digest reported that the house has 12 bedrooms, several outbuildings and a 60-foot-long beamed living hall. Rather than extensively modernising the property, Stewart embraced many of its existing details and furnishings. The property was sold to Stewart with much of its contents still inside. According to Architectural Digest, the purchase included cabinets and shelves containing the Fords’ silver, glassware, china and linens. Stewart herself told the magazine, “I didn’t have to buy a plate,” adding that she had nevertheless added her own pieces over the years. That approach helped retain a direct connection to the home's previous owners. Architectural Digest noted that Stewart has described herself as a caretaker of the property.Inside, Skylands retains numerous details associated with its early-20th-century design. These include Pewabic-tiled bathrooms, leaded-glass windows, polished copper, cut crystal and vintage Frigidaire refrigerators in the kitchen, along with furniture and decorative objects ranging from Georgian stools and wing chairs to regional maps and prewar prints of Maine birds.Stewart has added her own design touches, but they have generally been incorporated alongside the property's existing character. Architectural Digest reported that Kevin Sharkey, then executive editorial director at Martha Stewart Living, assisted her with the decorating. Some original objects have been stored, while others remain part of the home's interiors.The house also became a source of inspiration for Stewart's wider creative work. Architectural Digest reported that she spends part of July and August at Skylands, along with long weekends during other parts of the year, and that the property has served as a setting and inspiration for her design work and media projects.The restoration of Skylands has extended beyond the house itself. Stewart's 2013 blog post focused particularly on the work of Patrick Chassé and the challenge of recovering aspects of Jensen's original landscape design. She wrote that Jensen's work had used the existing vegetation and terrain to create a landscape that felt naturally integrated with the property. The estate's history also remains visible in its setting. Architectural Digest described pink-granite gravel drives winding through the forest, terraces surrounded by natural vegetation and a house constructed from local stone that appears to emerge from the surrounding granite landscape.The property had changed hands before Stewart acquired it. Architectural Digest reported that the Fords and their four children spent summers there until another family acquired the estate in 1980, following Eleanor Ford's death. That family subsequently sold Skylands to Stewart in 1997.Today, Skylands remains a private retreat for Stewart, but its significance extends beyond its role as a celebrity home. Its architecture, original furnishings and Jensen-designed landscape preserve links to the Ford family's era on Mount Desert Island. Stewart's approach has centred on maintaining those layers of history while continuing to use the estate as a living home rather than treating it solely as a preserved relic.
Article Summary: Skylands was developed for Edsel Ford, the son of Henry Ford, and his wife, Eleanor. The house was completed in 1925 and designed by architect Duncan Candler, while renowned landscape designer Jens Jensen created the surrounding landscape. Stewart bought the 63-acre estate in 1997, reportedly for just under $6 million, and has since treated the property as a piece of American architectural and landscape history.

Article Title: A Hanford landfill has taken 20 million tons of radioactive and hazardous waste since 1996; its latest expansion will add 2.8 million cubic yards
Article Text:
How ERDF handles waste from Hanford’s cleanup work

PC: DOE

20 million tons have gone through the facility

Hanford’s Super Cell 11 adds 2.8 million cubic yards of space

How ERDF is designed to contain water from the landfill

The landfill helping crews tackle Hanford’s legacy waste

At the centre of Washington state’s sprawling Hanford Site, an enormous engineered landfill is being made larger as one of the United States’ biggest environmental cleanup programmes continues. According to the US Department of Energy (DOE), the Environmental Restoration Disposal Facility (ERDF) has been receiving waste since 1996. Over that time, 20 million tons of material from cleanup operations have been placed there, including low-level radioactive and hazardous waste. Now, workers have finished excavating another section of the landfill. The new disposal cell is 80 feet deep and covers an area roughly 500 feet wide and 1,000 feet long. Once its protective liner is installed, it will provide another 2.8 million cubic yards of capacity.ERDF sits on the Central Plateau, close to the middle of the 580-square-mile Hanford Site. It was opened in 1996 to give crews carrying out environmental restoration somewhere to take certain solid wastes removed during the cleanup.Its contents are not limited to one type of material. The facility receives low-level radioactive waste, hazardous waste and mixed solid waste produced by Hanford cleanup projects.Contaminated soil, debris from demolished structures and material removed from old waste sites are among the types of waste that can be handled there.The distinction matters because Hanford has several different waste-management systems. Waste from the site's underground tanks, for example, follows separate storage, treatment and disposal routes. ERDF has a more specific job: dealing with qualifying solid material generated as contaminated areas and ageing facilities are cleaned up.Approximately 20 million tons of cleanup waste have been disposed of at ERDF, according to information from the US Department of Energy.As reported by Hanford Communities, that material has come from work involving more than 800 demolished facilities and about 1,300 waste sites. Moving it has also required a huge amount of transportation. Trucks supporting ERDF operations have travelled more than 30 million miles, a distance DOE describes as roughly equivalent to making 1,200 trips around the Earth.The landfill has not remained the same size throughout that period. Its capacity has been increased several times as cleanup work generated more material requiring disposal. Earlier expansions were completed in 1999, 2003, 2007 and 2011.Reportedly, the newest addition is being referred to as Super Cell 11. The description reflects its scale: the cell is about twice the size of the original disposal cells at the facility. Excavation began during the summer, eventually producing a cavity about 80 feet deep. Across the surface, it stretches approximately 500 feet from side to side and 1,000 feet in length. The completed cell is expected to provide around 2.8 million cubic yards of additional disposal space.That is capacity intended for future cleanup rather than a one-off project. DOE has said the expansion is expected to support the Hanford mission through at least 2040, giving contractors somewhere to manage qualifying solid waste as work continues across the site.Finishing the excavation does not mean the disposal cell is ready to receive waste. Contractors with the Central Plateau Cleanup Company (CPCCo) are due to complete the project by installing an engineered liner.Kelly Ebert, director for the Projects and Facilities Division with the US The Department of Energy Office of Environmental Management’s Hanford Field Office said, “ERDF has been a cornerstone of our waste disposal strategy for nearly 30 years, and this expansion is essential to provide uninterrupted, efficient and safe disposal for years to come.”The liner forms part of the system intended to keep potentially contaminated water from reaching the underlying environment. Rainfall, snowmelt and water used to control dust can enter the disposal area, so the engineered system is designed to collect that water and direct it towards holding tanks for treatment.Hanford's cleanup involves removing material from a site that was heavily used for nuclear weapons production during the 20th century. Much of the current work involves dealing with the physical remains of that history, including contaminated ground, old buildings and waste sites.ERDF gives those projects a central disposal point for waste that meets the facility's acceptance requirements. Instead of leaving contaminated soil or demolition material at the individual locations where it was found, cleanup teams can transport it to the engineered landfill.The scale of the facility reflects the scale of the wider operation. Its 107-acre footprint has already accommodated millions of tons of waste, while further cleanup work is expected to continue for years.
Article Summary: Hanford’s Super Cell 11 adds 2.8 million cubic yards of space to the landfill. The new disposal cell is 80 feet deep and covers an area roughly 500 feet wide and 1,000 feet long. The Environmental Restoration Disposal Facility (ERDF) has been receiving waste since 1996. 20 million tons of material from cleanup operations have been placed there.

Article Title: Dallas gave developers 10 more months to buy its 72-story Bank of America Plaza and keep $103 million in incentives tied to a $409 million plan adding a hotel, garage, restaurant and observation deck
Article Text:
The immediate priority is now completing the city's development agreement and closing the tower purchase before July 30, 2027.

A new deadline for a complex deal

A $409 million transformation

$103 million in public incentives

Downtown Dallas is changing

The road ahead

Downtown Dallas is betting that one of its most recognizable towers can have a second act. The developers behind a sweeping $409 million redevelopment of Bank of America Plaza have been given another 10 months to complete the purchase of the 72-story skyscraper, keeping more than $100 million in public incentives attached to the ambitious transformation, states a report by CRE Daily.According to CRE Daily report, the Dallas City Council has extended the purchase deadline to July 30, 2027, giving developers Mike Hoque and Mike Ablon additional time to finalize their acquisition of the tower and complete a development agreement with the city. The pair, operating as 901 Main PAHG Partners LLC, announced plans in 2024 to acquire the property from Metropolis Investment Holdings, a Chicago-based investment firm managing the asset for a German family investment group, adds the report.If we go by the report, the original closing deadline was September 30. The additional time reflects the complexity of a transaction that involves not only purchasing the building but also negotiating the public-private development agreement and the extensive redevelopment planned for the property.The acquisition itself is expected to cost more than $165 million. Once completed, the project would substantially change how the landmark tower is used, explains the online report.Office space would shrink from roughly 1.8 million square feet to 1.5 million square feet, with the remaining space undergoing a full renovation. The redevelopment would also introduce 275 hotel rooms, with the project targeting a four-star-or-better standard.A new glass-and-steel structure would house the hotel's lobby and ballroom, while a 1,115-space parking garage would replace a surface parking lot across the street. A skybridge over Main Street would connect the garage to the tower, confirms the report.At street level, the plans call for additional retail space. Higher up, the 69th floor would become home to a restaurant and observation deck, adding a destination component to one of Dallas' most visible buildings.The redevelopment is backed by significant public investment. Dallas City Council approved a $103 million payment from the Downtown Connection Tax Increment Financing district last October. The development team has already spent about $4 million on design work and says it has secured a capital partner and financing for the project, although financial details have not been disclosed. Earlier city documents projected completion as early as September 2032, confirms the report.The redevelopment comes as the city's traditional downtown office market undergoes a broader shift. Bank of America, the tower's longtime anchor tenant, is expected to move to a new Bank of America Tower at Parkside near Klyde Warren Park within the next few years. Other major changes are also reshaping Main Street. Neiman Marcus is preparing to close its century-old store at 1618 Main Street, while AT&T is moving its headquarters to Plano, although its lease at One Whitacre Tower runs through 2031.Bank of America Plaza is not the only downtown property facing pressure. The financial challenges surrounding older office towers, including 2100 Ross, have underscored the difficulties of repositioning aging commercial real estate. For Hoque and Ablon, the project is also their largest redevelopment undertaking to date. Earlier agreements involving Hoque in Fort Worth and Mansfield were terminated over missed deadlines, according to the Dallas Business Journal.The immediate priority is now completing the city's development agreement and closing the tower purchase before July 30, 2027. If the plan stays on schedule, the transformation could coincide with the redevelopment of the nearby Kay Bailey Hutchison Convention Center, a $3.5 billion-to-$3.8 billion project expected to bring additional activity to the western side of downtown.Images Courtesy: Wikipedia and istock
Article Summary: Developers Mike Hoque and Mike Ablon have been given another 10 months to complete the purchase of the 72-story skyscraper. The Dallas City Council has extended the purchase deadline to July 30, 2027. The acquisition itself is expected to cost more than $165 million.

Article Title: After more than 50 years of pulp-mill pollution, regulators have proposed restoring North Carolina's Roanoke River, including contaminated floodplain habitat damaged by toxic discharges
Article Text:
The Plymouth Mill began operating in 1937 as a wood and paper products manufacturing facility. Over subsequent decades, industrial operations at the site resulted in hazardous substances being released into groundwater, soil, Welch Creek and the Roanoke River (Image Credit: Domtar)

Decades of pollution affected the lower Roanoke River

Proposed plan would protect wetlands and reconnect floodplains

Previous actions have already reduced some impacts

Public can comment on the proposed restoration

For more than half a century, pollution from a pulp and paper mill has left its mark on North Carolina’s lower Roanoke River, affecting fish, wetlands and other natural resources. Now, a proposed restoration plan aims to address some of that long-term damage by protecting floodplain habitat, reconnecting historic waterways and improving conditions for fish and wildlife. According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), federal and state natural resource trustees have proposed restoration projects to compensate for injuries linked to hazardous-substance releases from the former Plymouth Mill. The proposal includes wetland conservation and habitat restoration across the lower Roanoke River system.The Plymouth Mill began operating in 1937 as a wood and paper products manufacturing facility. Over subsequent decades, industrial operations at the site resulted in hazardous substances being released into groundwater, soil, Welch Creek and the Roanoke River. Contaminants identified in the area include dioxins, furans, mercury and volatile organic compounds.The pollution affected aquatic ecosystems as contaminants accumulated in fish and other species. A fish consumption advisory associated with the contamination has remained in place for decades. The mill also withdrew water from the Roanoke River for its manufacturing operations, drawing larval fish into the facility and contributing to impacts on fish populations and recreational fishing. The mill's ownership has since changed. The facility is now owned by Domtar Paper Company, which assumed responsibility for addressing the site's environmental liabilities after acquiring the property from Weyerhaeuser. The proposed agreement involves Domtar funding or carrying out restoration measures to compensate for natural-resource injuries associated with the former mill's pollution.One of the central elements of the proposed restoration plan is the protection of approximately 760 acres of forested wetlands at Warren Neck through a conservation deed restriction. According to NOAA and North Carolina DEQ, the area provides fish nursery habitat that is important to the health of the Roanoke River.The proposal also includes about $1.75 million for floodplain reconnection, wetland protection and fish-passage improvements. The project could repair up to five lost natural connections by restoring habitat and installing water crossings and fish-friendly culverts. It is expected to reconnect about three miles of historic stream channels to their natural flow and flood regime while improving more than 600 acres of habitat. Together, these measures are intended to address natural-resource losses associated with the mill while protecting areas that support fish and other wildlife in the lower river system.The proposed restoration follows earlier efforts to address damage associated with the Plymouth Mill. Under the natural-resource damage assessment process, trustees previously selected measures aimed at reducing fish mortality caused by the mill's cooling-water intake. Domtar voluntarily implemented modifications that reduced the volume of water withdrawn from the Roanoke River. The company has also received proposed settlement credit for previous improvements to the Plymouth boat ramp and waterfront park, lighting improvements and the installation of high-capacity cooling-water towers that eliminated river withdrawals for cooling purposes.The pollution cleanup itself has also continued. According to Inside Climate News, Domtar has spent at least $5.5 million on remediation since 2011, including measures to contain contaminated sediment in Welch Creek.The restoration plan is part of a proposed consent decree submitted in federal court by the North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality, NOAA and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. The agreement is being pursued under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation and Liability Act, through the natural-resource damage assessment and restoration process. The proposed work would focus not only on individual contaminated areas but also on protecting and reconnecting the wider floodplain and aquatic habitat. The Roanoke River supports diverse fish populations and extensive bottomland forests, making the lower river an important ecological area.The restoration plan is currently subject to public review. NOAA's restoration programme has invited comments on the proposed projects, while the proposed consent decree is also undergoing the federal public-comment process. The agencies will consider comments before the proposed settlement and restoration measures move forward.
Article Summary: Proposed plan would protect wetlands and reconnect floodplains. Contaminants identified in the area include dioxins, furans, mercury and volatile organic compounds. Previous actions have already reduced some impacts of the pollution. Public can comment on the proposed restoration plan.

Article Title: 526 kg drugs worth Rs 3,000 crore seized from Iranian boat with Pakistani crew
Article Text:
Coast guard intercepts Iranian dhow, seizes 526 kg narcotics worth over Rs 3,000cr

NEW DELHI: The Indian Coast Guard , in coordination with the Gujarat Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS), seized approximately 526 kg of narcotics from an Iranian dhow in the Arabian Sea west of Lakshadweep, officials said.The Coast Guard said five Pakistani nationals operating the vessel were also detained during the operation carried out near Lakshadweep on September 25, as reported by news agency PTI.The drugs, valued at over Rs 3,000 crore in the international market, were seized after the vessel was intercepted during the operation.The Coast Guard conducted coordinated sea-air surveillance to track the suspicious vessel before launching a hot pursuit and boarding the dhow.The operation was carried out in coordination with the Gujarat Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS) to intercept the vessel. The seized contraband comprised heroin and methamphetamine, while five Pakistani nationals operating the dhow were also apprehended.The dhow, its crew and the seized drugs were escorted to Mumbai under armed security for joint interrogation and further legal proceedings.The operation was part of coordinated efforts by the Coast Guard and Gujarat ATS to detect and disrupt suspected transnational maritime drug-smuggling networks.The seizure comes as Indian maritime and law enforcement agencies continue efforts to prevent narcotics from being smuggled through sea routes. The Coast Guard has previously conducted joint operations with Gujarat ATS and other agencies to intercept vessels suspected of carrying illegal drugs.In April 2025, the Coast Guard, along with Gujarat ATS, seized 307.5 kg of narcotics off the Gujarat coast, according to the Coast Guard's official record of interdiction cases.Several drug-interdiction operations have been conducted along maritime routes in the Arabian Sea, with agencies relying on intelligence inputs, vessel surveillance and coordination between maritime and land-based enforcement units to identify suspected consignments.The Coast Guard said the latest operation underlined its efforts to strengthen maritime surveillance and prevent illicit activities in India's maritime zones. The seized drugs and apprehended crew were brought to Mumbai for further investigation and legal action.
Article Summary: Indian Coast Guard intercepts Iranian dhow, seizes 526 kg narcotics worth over Rs 3,000cr. The seized contraband comprised heroin and methamphetamine. Five Pakistani nationals operating the dhow were also apprehended. The seizure comes as Indian maritime and law enforcement agencies continue efforts to prevent narcotics from being smuggled.

Article Title: Russia backs India's claim to UNSC seat, firmly shuts door on Germany & Japan
Article Text:
Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov addresses the 81st United Nations General Assembly (Photo: Reuters).

Russia on Saturday backed a permanent seat for India and Brazil on the United Nations Security Council, while strongly opposing the same for Western countries.During his speech at the General Assembly, Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov said no additional seats at the UNSC should be given to Western countries, especially to Germany and the US ally, Japan.Russia has been one of the most consistent supporters of India’s bid for a permanent seat on the UN Security Council . Moscow has repeatedly backed India’s candidature as part of a broader push to make the Council more representative of Asia, Africa and Latin America.Lavrov has previously argued that the current composition no longer reflects today’s global balance and explicitly endorsed India, alongside Brazil, for permanent membership.This support was reiterated in the 2026 BRICS New Delhi Declaration, with China and Russia backing India and Brazil for a greater role in the UN, including the Security Council.Lavrov accused the West of continuously pumping weapons into Ukraine while helping target drones and missiles at Russia's civilians and civilian infrastructure.He also mentioned that Europe raised an anti-Moscow regime in Kyivv, in order to control the Russian influence."To pursue a utopian goal of containing Russia, the West dismantled the European security system and cultivated a Russophobic regime in Kyiv," he said, while warning the Western nations of "consequences".He further accused Europe of doing everything to block a peaceful settlement with Ukraine and disrupt negotiation prospects favoured by many, including the Trump administration.Lavrov claimed several EU leaders of being infected with racial superiority, encouraging the rise of what he called Ukrainian Nazism.The Russian foreign minister said the UN’s core principles were being put at risk, with the West overlooking the spread of Nazism in Ukraine.
Article Summary: Russia has been one of the most consistent supporters of India's bid for a permanent seat on the UN Security Council. Moscow has repeatedly backed India’s candidature as part of a broader push to make the Council more representative of Asia, Africa and Latin America.

Article Title: Student protests rock France with over 400 detained: Why are schools protesting - explained
Article Text:
File photo: A student walks past a burning bicycle next to the Baggio High School, blocked in protest of the government's release of next year's draft budget, in Lille, France

Students take protests beyond Paris

Civil servants join nationwide strike

Why the budget is at the centre of the anger

Poll Vote & Share your view Which area should receive greater priority in France’s upcoming budget? Education Healthcare Public Safety Infrastructure 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

France was hit by a nationwide wave of strikes and student protests, with civil servants walking off the job and high school students blocking hundreds of schools as anger over budget cuts, overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages spread across the country.The mobilisation came two days before Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu's government is due to present its draft 2027 budget, which includes a planned €54 billion savings drive. The protests have added to pressure on the government as it tries to rein in France's finances ahead of next year's presidential election.The unrest was particularly visible at schools, where students piled up bins and barriers to prevent access. The education ministry said around 400 schools were affected by protests or disruptions on Tuesday, out of roughly 3,700 nationwide. More than 440 people, most of them minors, were detained, according to interior minister Laurent Nuñez.​​At least 10 teachers, several students and 48 law enforcement officers were also injured during Tuesday's unrest, according to officials.The school protests began in the Paris region last week but have since spread to cities including Lille, Lyon, Nantes, Marseille, Bordeaux and Rennes.Students have been protesting over a shortage of teachers, overcrowded classrooms, poor school conditions and demanding timetables. At some schools, however, the demonstrations escalated into clashes with police.In Lille, rubbish bins were set on fire outside the Lycée César Baggio, while police used tear gas and batons after protesters threw objects. Similar confrontations were reported elsewhere, although many blockades remained peaceful.At the Lycée Arago in Paris, students blocked the entrance with bins while a placard reading "Macron explosion" was displayed. Outside the Hélène-Boucher school, protesters put up a banner saying "Fewer cops, More money"."We want fewer police because we think there is a huge amount of police repression, both against high school student movements and social movements more generally," final-year student Mael Breton told Reuters.Students have cited teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and poor school conditions as key grievances. “There are 34 of us in each class, and it’s just not feasible. The teachers are overworked,” a 16-year-old student told AFP, saying the education system was “completely broken.”The government's response has been mixed. Lecornu condemned violence around schools but acknowledged that students' concerns over the education system needed to be heard and addressed. Education minister Édouard Geffray said students had a right to protest but condemned violence as "indefensible".The student mobilisation coincided with a broader strike by public-sector workers, including teachers, healthcare workers and firefighters.Unions organised more than 170 rallies across France to oppose the government's budget plans and its proposed freeze on state employees' base salaries in 2027. The CGT union has argued that repeated pay freezes have eroded workers' purchasing power.Firefighters were among those taking part after a summer of major wildfires exposed concerns over resources. The education ministry said just over 11% of teachers and other school staff were on strike, while participation among other civil servants was below 10%.Transport disruption was limited in the morning, although the aviation regulator warned of possible disruption at some airports.CGT leader Sophie Binet said the government had 48 hours to reverse the planned spending cuts before the union considers further strike action."This summer, who was on the front line? It wasn't the billionaires, the big bosses or the shareholders. It was civil servants and working people. And how are they being thanked? By cutting their pay? The anger is enormous," she told BFMTV.Lecornu's government is trying to find savings as France grapples with a mounting debt burden. The proposed €54 billion savings package is aimed at bringing the public deficit down, while the government has also warned that public debt could reach 121.7% of GDP in 2027.France's public debt reached €3.595 trillion at the end of June, or around 119% of GDP, according to national statistics agency Insee.The cost of servicing that debt is also rising. France is expected to spend around €79 billion on interest payments this year, with the government projecting the figure could rise to €91 billion in 2027.The government is therefore trying to cut spending while unions resist pay restraint and students demand more teachers and resources for schools.
Article Summary: Around 400 schools were affected by protests or disruptions on Tuesday. More than 440 people, most of them minors, were detained, interior minister says. At least 10 teachers, several students and 48 law enforcement officers were also injured. Unions organised more than 170 rallies across France.

Article Title: ‘Wake up’: Iran releases 25-page letter urging US voters to reject Trump ahead of midterms
Article Text:
The letter was released about five weeks before the US midterm elections

‘Wake up’: Iran takes message to US voters

‘Death to America’ explained as attack on rulers

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe that Iran's appeal to American voters will influence the outcome of the midterm elections? Yes, it will have a significant impact No, it will not influence the elections Possibly, but only to a limited extent 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has made a direct appeal to American voters, urging them to reject President Donald Trump ’s policies and “wrest control back from corrupt politicians” as the US heads towards its midterm elections. In a lengthy open letter addressed to the American public, the powerful Iranian military force argued that Washington’s war against Iran had failed to achieve its objectives and called for a change in US policy towards Tehran.The 25-page letter, released seven months after the US-Israel war against Iran began, seeks to draw a distinction between the American people and their government. The IRGC argues that ordinary Iranians and Americans share common interests and grievances, portraying both as victims of political leaders pursuing costly wars. It also urges Americans to oppose US support for Israel and foreign military interventions, while presenting peaceful coexistence between Washington and Tehran as possible if US policy changes.IRGC spokesman Gen Hossein Mohebbi reinforced the message at a news conference in Tehran on Tuesday, saying the only way for the conflict to end was for Washington to acknowledge defeat and withdraw. He urged Americans to reconsider their leadership and put pressure on the Trump administration, arguing that many US citizens remained unaware of what he described as the “harms” caused by its policies.The timing of the letter is significant. The letter was released about five weeks before the US midterm elections, with the IRGC describing the current period as a moment when the American political system is at its weakest. Mohebbi said he did not necessarily expect the letter to change the US administration’s behaviour, but hoped American voters would hear its message.The letter repeatedly attacks Trump’s justification for the war, particularly his claim that Iran’s nuclear programme posed a threat that required military action. Tehran has consistently denied seeking nuclear weapons and maintains that its uranium enrichment programme has civilian purposes.“The enemy [US] knows that Iran is not after nuclear weapons,” Mohebbi said, echoing the letter’s argument that Washington has used the nuclear issue as a pretext to pursue wider strategic and economic goals.The IRGC also claims that the US and Israel failed to achieve their stated objectives in the war. According to the letter, the targets shifted repeatedly after earlier goals, including regime change and partition of Iran, were not achieved. It lists objectives ranging from forcing Iran’s unconditional surrender and destroying its nuclear and missile programmes to taking control of the Strait of Hormuz.The letter declares Iran the victor, claiming that thousands of US and Israeli strikes damaged Iranian infrastructure but failed to accomplish their stated aims. It further claims that Iranian forces inflicted major losses on US military assets and severely damaged American bases across the region. These assertions are presented by the IRGC as evidence of a broader strategic defeat for Washington.The Strait of Hormuz features prominently in the letter and Mohebbi’s remarks. He rejected US claims that Iran had lost its leverage over the vital waterway, arguing that the movement of a limited number of vessels did not mean the strait was fully open. Oil exports through the waterway, however, have recovered substantially from the levels seen earlier in the conflict, according to figures cited in the supplied material.The IRGC letter also attempts to explain one of the most recognisable slogans associated with Iran’s political system: “Death to America”. It argues that the phrase is directed at the US political establishment rather than the American population.“‘Death to America’ is a prayer for the eradication of the diabolical ruling elite whose seat of power is the White House,” the letter says.The document repeatedly contrasts the American public with Washington’s political leadership, claiming that taxpayers ultimately bear the financial burden of US wars. It asks Americans to question why their government continues to pursue military confrontation and warns of what it describes as the consequences of an ongoing conflict.The IRGC’s approach echoes Cold War-era efforts to reach an adversary’s population directly. During the Vietnam War, Vietnamese broadcaster Trinh Thi Ngo, widely known as “Hanoi Hannah”, used English-language broadcasts to target American troops, urging them to question their government and the war. Her programmes highlighted US casualties, anti-war protests and reports critical of the conflict while presenting the Vietnamese side’s narrative.Iran has similarly sought to communicate directly with Western audiences since the latest war began, using Iran-linked media and online networks, including English-language AI-generated videos, memes and short-form content.The IRGC letter now represents a much more formal version of that strategy: an attempt to speak past Washington and directly to American voters.For Tehran, the central message is that the war is not simply a military confrontation between two states, but a political choice that Americans themselves can challenge. Mohebbi urged them to put pressure on their government, while the letter concluded with a broader argument that Iran’s resistance had demonstrated the limits of American military power.Meanwhile, Iran’s economic pressures remain severe. The rial fell to a new record low on Tuesday, with traders in Tehran reportedly exchanging more than 2.5 million rials for one US dollar. The currency has repeatedly hit new lows since the war began.
Article Summary: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has made a direct appeal to American voters, urging them to reject President Donald Trump ’s policies. The 25-page letter, released seven months after the US-Israel war against Iran began, seeks to draw a distinction between the American people and their government. The IRGC argues that ordinary Iranians and Americans share common interests and grievances.

Article Title: In 2024, 75-year-old Iowa farmer Evie Haupt said three wind turbines on her 160 acres were bringing in about $35,000 a year while using under 3 acres and had helped reduce $350,000 in farm debt to $67
Article Text:
A financial lifeline for rural landowners

The explosive expansion of Iowa wind power

Addressing local pushback and debate

On a 160-acre farm in central Iowa, three tall wind turbines quietly rise above the fields. Each turbine uses less than an acre of land, but together they provide an annual income that has changed the financial future of 75-year-old farmer Evie Haupt. According to a CBS News report by Janet Shamlian and Alicia Hastey, Haupt earns about $35,000 each year by leasing part of her land for the wind turbines. The income rises with inflation and has helped her pay down a $350,000 farm debt left after her husband died a decade ago. Her remaining debt is now $67,000. For many family farms across the United States, extra sources of income have become important lifelines. The U.S. Department of Agriculture expects farm profits to fall by 25 per cent, as farmers face higher costs, changing crop prices and unpredictable weather. Adding wind power to traditional farming can provide steady income and help protect farmers from financial shocks.Farm debt can leave families with difficult choices, including selling land that has been in the family for generations. Haupt faced this situation after her husband died and left her with hundreds of thousands of dollars in farm debt.Payments from the wind turbines provided her with a regular source of income that she could use to repay the loans. Each turbine takes up less than an acre, allowing Haupt to continue farming most of her 160 acres. This means the same land provides her with two sources of income while only a small portion is used for the turbines. The payments can also increase over time because the contracts include inflation adjustments, helping landowners manage rising prices and other costs. For Haupt, the arrangement has made a significant difference. She has now paid off more than 80% of her farm debt while continuing to use the land for farming.Iowa has become a major wind energy state over the past two decades. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, Iowa had only a few hundred wind turbines 20 years ago. Today, it has more than 6,000, producing about 60 per cent of the state's energy. Across the United States, more than 70,000 land-based wind turbines are operating, according to the U.S. Department of Energy. Nationwide, wind power supplies about 10 per cent of the electric grid. Federal energy officials also say current U.S. wind power cuts carbon emissions by an amount equal to taking 73 million passenger vehicles off the road. Attorney Kathy Law, who grew up on a farm and married a farmer, has helped place nearly half of Iowa's wind turbines. Her work in energy law grew from her own family's experience with farming. Law wanted to study law while she was in high school, but the severe farm crisis of the 1980s kept her home to help with the family farm. She later went to law school in her forties. She graduated on the same day her son finished high school and later served as president of the Iowa Wind Energy Association for three years. "From my farm background, I think I can talk their talk and have conversations with landowners that are interested in having wind turbines on their property," Law told CBS News.The rapid growth of wind power in rural communities has also brought opposition in some counties. Local critics say wind turbines can change scenic views, create unwanted noise and threaten birds and bats. Law believes landowners should be able to decide what happens on their property. "Nobody's requiring them to put that on their farms or on their land," Law said during her interview with CBS News. "We want to be able to put turbines on our land and receive those benefits. " Haupt has a similar view of the changes to her farm. While she remains attached to traditional farming, she sees clean energy as an important step for rural communities. "I look at it as progress," Haupt told CBS News. "I think we can't stand in the way of progress." For Haupt, giving up a very small part of her land to produce electricity makes sense for her finances and for the wider community. "I need to give up one or two acres of my land so that I can generate a commodity that we all use every day, and we all want to use more of it every day," Haupt said. "So I'm happy to be able to be a part of that generation."
Article Summary: Iowa has become a major wind energy state over the past two decades. More than 70,000 land-based wind turbines are operating in the U.S. Nationwide, wind power supplies about 10 per cent of the electric grid. Critics say wind turbines change scenic views, create unwanted noise and threaten birds and bats.

Article Title: In 1992, California finished removing feral goats from San Clemente Island; a rare native plant later rebounded to more than 3,500 individuals
Article Text:
Representative image of goats grazing along a rugged coastal landscape. Image Credits: ChatGPT.

How grazing reshaped the island

The paintbrush begins to return

The San Clemente Island paintbrush was once fairly common, but intensive grazing sharply reduced its numbers. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

Recovery did not mean the work was over

On San Clemente Island, off the coast of Southern California, an unlikely conservation story unfolded after one of the island's most damaging pressures was finally removed. Feral goats had grazed across the island for generations, stripping vegetation, trampling the ground, and causing erosion. Among the plants affected was the San Clemente Island paintbrush (Castilleja grisea), a small perennial found nowhere else.According to Annals of Botany , by the time the goats and other non-native grazing animals had been removed in the early 1990s, the San Clemente Island paintbrush had become extremely rare. Once grazing pressure ended, the plant began reappearing in areas where it had been difficult to find. Surveys in the late 1990s recorded more than 3,500 individuals, consistent with a substantial recovery after goat removal.San Clemente Island had been extensively used by livestock for many years. Sheep, cattle, pigs, and goats had been brought to the island, and the grazing practices over decades damaged the native vegetation. In addition to eating vegetation, the livestock trampled plants and carved trails that contributed to soil erosion. The goats were difficult to remove because they could survive in the island’s rugged terrain and hide in inaccessible areas.According to the Santa Barbara Botanic Garden , the US Navy began an organised feral-goat eradication programme in 1972, working with other organisations to remove goats from San Clemente Island over the following decades. As the population became smaller and more difficult to locate, the programme later used the "Judas goat" technique, in which radio-collared goats helped researchers find groups of goats that remained in remote areas. Between 1989 and 1991, 263 goats were killed during this later phase of the eradication effort. By 1992, the remaining non-native ungulates had been removed from the island, ending decades of grazing pressure on its native vegetation.The San Clemente Island paintbrush was once fairly common, but intensive grazing sharply reduced its numbers. In 1977, it was placed on the federal endangered species list. By the late 1970s, only a few plants were known to remain. But the situation changed once the goats disappeared from the scene. Research published in Annals of Botany also notes that the plant began to rebound after the goats were removed, with more than 3,500 individuals counted in the late 1990s. Scientists studying the plant’s genetics noted fairly high genetic diversity despite its long period of scarcity.Surveys in 1996 and 1997 recorded 77 populations and about 3,500 individual plants. Later surveys found even larger numbers. From 2003 to 2006, researchers recorded 198 populations containing an estimated 9,718 individual plants. Vegetation around San Clemente Island also recovered after the feral goats were eradicated, with native plants able to persist in areas that were previously exposed to heavy grazing pressure.The removal of the goats took away one of the greatest pressures that the paintbrush faced, but it was not the only problem. The plant’s recovery took place amid concerns about soil erosion, invasive plants, fire, land use, and military activity. The US Fish and Wildlife Service has noted that some of the plant's current distribution may reflect areas where steep terrain once protected it from goats. Seeds may also have remained in the soil, allowing the species to recolonise areas after grazing ended. This suggests the recovery had multiple contributing factors, though removing non-native herbivores addressed the primary threat identified when the plant was listed.Nevertheless, the plant’s recovery was strong enough to prompt a change in its legal status. The San Clemente Island paintbrush was delisted from the endangered species list in 2023. The US Fish and Wildlife Service says the species recovered after non-native herbivores were removed. Once grazing pressure ended, the plant had a chance to grow again. The plant recovered from a small number to thousands.
Article Summary: The San Clemente Island paintbrush (Castilleja grisea) was once fairly common, but intensive grazing sharply reduced its numbers. Feral goats had grazed across the island for generations, stripping vegetation, trampling the ground, and causing erosion. The US Navy began an organised feral-goat eradication programme in 1972. By 1992, the remaining non-native ungulates had been removed from the island, ending decades of grazing pressure on its native vegetation. The plant recovered from a small number to thousands.

Article Title: In 2006, a floating-home resident challenged Riviera Beach’s $2.4 billion waterfront redevelopment plan; the city later abandoned it
Article Text:
Representative image of a floating-home resident aboard his houseboat as a proposed waterfront redevelopment threatens the marina community. Image Credits: ChatGPT.

A waterfront redevelopment plan meets a new law

From redevelopment opponent to courtroom defendant

In 2006, Fane Lozman took a stand against a grand waterfront development initiative in Riviera Beach, Florida, which aimed to utilise eminent domain to seize homes for the project. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

The floating home reaches the Supreme Court

In 2006, a small floating home in Riviera Beach, Florida, became central to a larger fight over land, redevelopment and local government power. Fane Lozman had moved his houseboat into the city-owned marina when he discovered that Riviera Beach was planning a $2.4 billion waterfront redevelopment project. The proposal called for acquiring about 2,200 homes and businesses, along with the marina, through eminent domain and transferring the properties to a private developer.According to the University of Miami Law Review , Lozman became an outspoken opponent of the redevelopment plan and challenged the city's actions surrounding the proposed project. Lozman objected publicly to the plan and challenged how the city approved its agreement with the developer. Within months, the redevelopment scheme was abandoned. It developed into a series of court battles that eventually took Lozman and his unusual home to the US Supreme Court.For several years, Riviera Beach had been pursuing a major redevelopment of its waterfront. The proposed project, estimated at $2.4 billion at the time, was intended to transform the marina area through private development.Plans included commercial and residential properties, as well as facilities for visitors and yachts. The redevelopment was also affected by changes to Florida's eminent-domain laws. State lawmakers passed House Bill 1567 on May 4, 2006, restricting the use of eminent domain for economic-development purposes, and Gov. Jeb Bush signed the legislation into law on May 11. In the middle of this process, on May 10, the Riviera Beach City Council agreed to work with Viking Inlet Harbour Properties as the project's master developer. By November 2006, however, the city had abandoned the waterfront redevelopment scheme.Lozman’s resistance to the plan led him to attend Riviera Beach City Council meetings frequently. His lawsuit over the development agreement led to further conflict with the city. In one case, Lozman was described as a loudmouth criticising the redevelopment project and alleging wrongdoing by city officials. Later, the city attempted to remove Lozman from the marina. One dispute concerned the terms of his marina residency.The dispute also drew academic attention. As the University of Miami Law Review notes, the redevelopment controversy came before the dispute over Lozman’s floating home and formed part of the background to his ongoing conflict with Riviera Beach. The city later filed a separate federal suit arguing that the floating home was a vessel subject to federal admiralty law. It was a 60-by-12-foot two-story wooden home consisting of a kitchen, bathroom, bedroom, and office space.According to the Florida Law Review , the legal significance of the case extended beyond the unusual appearance of Lozman's home. The dispute eventually reached the US Supreme Court, which ruled in 2013 that Lozman's floating home was not a vessel under federal maritime law. The justices said the key question was whether a reasonable observer would see the structure as designed to a practical degree to transport people or things over water. Because the home lacked features associated with maritime transport and was designed as a residence, the court ruled in Lozman’s favour. The decision established a “reasonable observer” test for determining vessel status, though later cases raised questions about how consistently it could be applied.However, Lozman’s legal disputes with Riviera Beach did not end with the 2013 ruling. In 2018, the Supreme Court said the lower court had used the wrong test to evaluate Lozman’s retaliation claim and sent the case back for further proceedings. What began as a dispute over waterfront redevelopment grew into a long legal history involving eminent domain, open-government laws, free speech and maritime law. The $2.4 billion project was abandoned in 2006, but the legal disputes surrounding Lozman’s floating house continued for years and reached the US Supreme Court more than once.
Article Summary: In 2006, Fane Lozman moved his houseboat into the city-owned marina in Riviera Beach, Florida. The city was planning a $2.4 billion waterfront redevelopment project. Lozman objected publicly to the plan and challenged how the city approved its agreement with the developer. The dispute eventually reached the US Supreme Court, which ruled in 2013 that Lozman's floating home was not a vessel under federal maritime law. In 2018, the Supreme Court said the lower court had used the wrong test to evaluate Lozman’s retaliation claim.

Article Title: In 2005 Ohio put ground tire rubber into 1 mile of King Road in Sylvania; 10 years later, the recycled section still matched the control at an 87% rating
Article Text:
AI-generated representative image showing ground tire rubber being incorporated into asphalt during a road resurfacing project. Credits - Gemini

How King Road became a test section

The 87% rating was kept

AI-generated representative image showing engineers inspecting a long-used pavement section made with recycled tire rubber. Credits - Gemini

What the outcome shows

On one side of the road, engineers applied a one-inch layer of ground tyre rubber as an asphalt overlay, while on the other side, a polymer-modified asphalt portion served as the control. The design of both blends met the Ohio Department of Transportation's requirements. The tyre rubber part and the control had the same pavement condition rating in every year reported in the study, which was a noteworthy outcome of ten years of monitoring. After four years, the rating reached 87%, and during the ten-year observation period, it barely altered. Rubber-modified asphalt is not always superior, according to the test. It has been shown that recycled tyre rubber can create a pavement section with long-term performance comparable to the conventional control under the conditions on King Road.The project uses the existing flexible pavement on King Road, Sylvania. The Ohio field report published through the U.S. Department of Transportation research archive says the new surface was a one-inch overlay applied in 2005 across a one-mile stretch.Different asphalt binders were used in the northbound and southbound lanes. One lane employed a modified binder of tyre rubber, or GTR. The control part used a polymer-modified binder. Both were PG rated 76-22 and were formulated to fulfil Ohio DOT criteria for fine-graded asphalt mixes.The road wasn’t a super-heavy truck route. The analysis revealed that the average daily traffic is roughly 7,120 cars per day, of which about 142 are trucks per day. That is important since pavement performance is highly dependent on traffic, climate and the structure underneath the surface. Researchers then followed the two sections rather than judging them after the first few seasons. Their records covered performance and pavement distress over a full decade, allowing the comparison to show how the rubber-modified mix behaved as cracking and other damage developed.The most popping number from the project is the 87% pavement condition rating. After four years, the PCR increased to 87% and then remained fairly steady, while the GTR and polymer-modified parts had the same PCR score in all years studied, according to the research. There were no cracks in the pavement. Transverse cracks emerged after around 2 years; non-wheel-track longitudinal cracks after 4 years. The fissures became more severe with time. The fourth year was the moment when crack sealing was required. Still, the two parts moved closer together. The study followed both for 10 years and found them to perform well with no significant difference in the pavement condition assessment.These conclusions are further validated by a separate long-term assessment of many Ohio GTR programs. The King Road project was one of the comparisons with a polymer-modified control, and 10-year field data were part of the study on GTR asphalt performance and life-cycle costs.Road authorities can use material from discarded tyres to add tyre rubber to asphalt for building of pavements. Ground rubber can change the properties of the asphalt binder, but the ultimate result relies on the rubber, binder, aggregate, mix design, traffic and climate. King Road is thus a representative field example, not a universal formula. The good 10-year performance in the Ohio research itself may have been due to the increased asphalt content used in the combinations on King Road and the relatively low traffic flow on that road.The finding is nevertheless remarkable because the rubber piece didn’t only survive a few years. Over a decade of service, it remained equivalent to the polymer-modified control while reaching the same 87% PCR level. The comparison is especially important because both sides of the road have similar surroundings and traffic. The use of a control section was employed in an effort to assess if the rubber-modified surface was deviating from normal polymer-modified pavement rather than assessing its condition alone.The Ohio research subsequently incorporated the topic into a larger study of GTR pavement performance. That means the King Road project is a real-world test of recycled material against a conventional option. While the road didn't prove all tire-rubber pavement can last 10 years, it did indicate that in this particular one-mile stretch of Sylvania, the recycled method can hold its own over time.
Article Summary: Engineers applied a one-inch layer of ground tyre rubber as an asphalt overlay. On the other side, a polymer-modified asphalt portion served as the control. The tyre rubber part and the control had the same pavement condition rating in every year reported in the study.

Article Title: In the 1970s, Newark Airport buried coal fly ash beneath runways built for jumbo jets; more than 20 years later, FHWA said the pavement was still performing well
Article Text:
AI-generated representative image showing a stabilized fly-ash base being constructed. Credits - Gemini

How the airport used the ash

Extended field test

AI-generated representative image showing an engineering core sample from an airport pavement with the stabilized base layer examined after years of service. Credits - Gemini

Importance of the Newark Experiment

The pavement must withstand repeated loads without failing or deforming when airports construct runways for huge planes. Throughout the 1970s, Newark International Airport in New Jersey hosted one of the biggest US operations using coal fly ash in a stabilised pavement base. The stuff wasn't just thrown underground. To make a cementitious base for flexible pavement, engineers used fly ash, lime, Portland cement, and sand. After 20 years or more, the Federal Highway Administration reported that the stabilised parts were still operating satisfactorily. This project was notable because it showed that a material derived from the burning of coal could be made into a structural layer for a large airport. It also provided an early example of the use of an industrial byproduct in the construction of long-life infrastructure.In the early to mid-1970s, construction began at Newark to build or expand runways, taxiways, and aircraft aprons for the jumbo jet era. Federal Highway Administration research on stabilised fly-ash bases indicates that the system was built as a flexible pavement with a stabilised base underneath. The basis was built in three levels with slightly varying mix compositions.Fly ash was 10 to 12% of the mix, and lime and Portland cement were roughly 3 to 4%. The completed stabilised base was 24 to 36 inches deep and provided a major structural layer beneath the asphalt surface of the runway system.The combination used a reaction between the fly ash and the activating ingredients. The reaction caused a cementitious matrix to form that linked the aggregate together, giving the base properties more akin to a layer of low-strength concrete than loose fill. This type of system is called a pozzolan-stabilized base by the FHWA, which is intended to offer load-bearing support under a flexible pavement.The design must also fulfil the requirements for heavier aircraft. The FHWA record shows one mixture with 4% lime and Portland cement reached ultimate strengths of roughly 2,000 to 2,600 pounds per square inch, suggesting the material was being employed as an engineered pavement component rather than as a simple waste-disposal approach.What makes the Newark experiment especially interesting is that the material had to show itself throughout years of use, not simply in laboratory tests. The FHWA's later examination indicated that the stabilized-base pavement sections appeared to be functioning satisfactorily after more than 20 years of operation. That finding is part of a longer history of using fly ash in pavement bases. The FHWA said stabilized-base compositions containing fly ash have been utilised in the United States since the 1950s, when the material reacts with lime, Portland cement or other activators to generate a binding matrix.The FDA also warned that the system has a flaw: cracking. Stabilised bases may have shrinkage fractures that will eventually reflect through the asphalt surface and increase maintenance requirements. This scenario means that long-term performance depends not only on the mix strength but also on the design, curing, and placement of the base.FHWA's guidance says that the proper mix depends on the type of fly ash, the type of aggregate, the activator, and the moisture conditions. Thus, the Newark experience was not evidence that any coal ash could be easily replaced in a runway. It demonstrated that a carefully formulated blend could operate under challenging conditions.Coal fly ash used to be considered primarily as a waste product that needed to be disposed of after coal was burnt. Alternatively, it may be used in stabilised pavement bases, putting part of that material into a regulated engineering use where its chemical qualities can add strength. That idea mattered economically as well. FHWA's study has shown that stabilised fly-ash bases usually have been more economical than other base materials in many places, however actual savings will depend on local resources, mix design and building conditions.The initiative also demonstrated the importance of linking material reuse to engineering and not simply substitution. Fly ash varies by source, and its behaviour depends on chemical composition and the activator used. The FHWA advice treats the material as part of a planned stabilized-base system with mix proportions, curing and strength development all influencing performance. That at Newark was particularly apparent, since the pavement was built to carry jumbo-jet loads. Even more than 20 years later, the government evaluation still said the stabilised pavement was performing satisfactorily.The lesson isn't that fly ash makes better runways automatically. It is that an industrial by-product can be turned into a valuable construction material if its chemistry, proportions and long-term behaviour are known. The runway base at Newark is one of the most obvious historic examples of that method in a major US airport project.
Article Summary: Newark International Airport in New Jersey used coal fly ash in a stabilised pavement base. After 20 years or more, the stabilised parts were still operating satisfactorily. The project was notable because it showed that a material derived from the burning of coal could be made into a structural layer for a large airport.

Article Title: California removed invasive rabbits from Santa Barbara Island; its endangered native dudleya stopped declining, with 534 plants later counted
Article Text:
Santa Barbara Island in California and an image of a hare. Credits - Wikimedia Commons

A plant on the verge

Santa Barbara Island Dudleya (Dudleya traskiae). Credits - Wikimedia Commons

Threats that remain

There are plants and creatures unique to the Channel Islands off the coast of southern California. Santa Barbara Island, about one square mile in area and home to plant species found only on the Channel Islands, illustrates the vulnerability of isolated island ecosystems. Over the course of more than a century, a large portion of its native vegetation was removed by goats, sheep, farms, and eventually rabbits.One fatality was the Santa Barbara Island liveforever, a succulent found nowhere else. Rabbits, often called hares in older accounts, chewed it so heavily that botanists feared in the early 1970s that it might be extinct. The National Park Service began removing an estimated 6,000 rabbits in 1954 and continued control efforts until the last rabbits were eliminated in 1981. The plant's decline subsequently stabilized, with 534 plants recorded around Signal Peak in 1984, 2,353 counted island-wide in 2020 and about 3,800 recorded in 2024. It remains classified as endangered.Dudleya traskiae, the liveforever, has rosettes of thick, pale green leaves and produces yellow flowers from spring into early summer. It grows on steep rocky slopes and sea cliffs surrounding the rim of the island.Earlier grazing by goats and sheep, followed by introduced rabbits and hares, severely altered the island's native vegetation. In the next decades came hares and rabbits. In 1950, a biologist identified only two rabbits, but by 1953 he reported that native vegetation had been damaged almost to the extent caused by earlier sheep grazing.By April 1978, when the US Fish and Wildlife Service designated the plant as endangered, only two populations were known to exist. One showed three plants coming out from stubs eaten down by animals to ground level; the other was a few hundred plants on a sea cliff out of reach of the creatures. A later Fish and Wildlife Service assessment, citing a 1975 Smithsonian report, said the plant had not been collected since 1968 and was considered possibly extinct. The listing blamed hares, but further investigation revealed the animals were actually rabbits. Now that the grazing was finished, the question was, how many plants were left?The last rabbits left in 1981, and park workers inspected the island in 1982, 1983, and 1984, discovering eleven colonies. The cliffs at Signal Peak were the only place where more than 100 plants were found, and discoveries in 1984 increased the estimate for that region to 534, according to a Fish and Wildlife Service evaluation of the species. In a three-year study from 1985 to 1987, the plants in its sample plots were found to be virtually steady, while the overall number of rosettes increased by 22%.Subsequent estimates were low but promising, numbering 852 plants island-wide in 2004 and 928 in 2006. The assessment cautioned that such numbers depended on assumptions about the cliffs at Signal Peak, so a real increase from one year to the next couldn’t be shown. Recruitment has been a perennial issue. Deer mice eat the seeds; dryness kills the seedlings, and when park officials planted roughly 800 seedlings in 2005, just 15 per cent survived until January 2006. More recent surveys have recorded substantially higher numbers, although the assessment notes uncertainty caused by different survey methods and the difficulty of counting plants on steep terrain.A later Fish and Wildlife Service assessment reported that 2020 surveys counted 2,353 plants, the highest total recorded to date. Most, 1,683, were in one stand visible only in aerial photos, meaning those plants had probably been there for years and uncounted. The study found no obvious overall pattern, with some colonies expanding and others contracting or dying, and it maintained the listing as an endangered species.The rabbit problem has largely been resolved, but other pressures remain. Native deer mice devour seeds, seedlings and mature plants, and 506 young plants planted out near the island’s dwellings and campsite in July 2019 had all disappeared by 2020, likely eaten by mice. Brown pelicans can also damage rosettes and alter the soil in ways that favor grasses. The assessment also identified introduced annual grasses and iceplant, along with fire risk, as continuing pressures on the species. They increased their roosting on the island from around 2004 onwards. Introduced annual grasses and iceplants continue to dominate most of the area, boosting both competition and fire risk. Conservationists have already collected seed and grown hundreds of seedlings on an island nursery. The assessment calls for regular monitoring and protective cages for fresh plantings.The available evidence suggests the rabbit removal helped the plant recover, although it was not the only factor. The species persisted after the rabbits were eliminated, new colonies were identified and later surveys recorded substantially more plants than earlier counts. But regeneration on a small, devastated island is gradual, and the future of the plant rests on managing mice, pelicans, weeds and fire as carefully as the rabbits once were.
Article Summary: Dudleya traskiae, the liveforever, has rosettes of thick, pale green leaves and produces yellow flowers from spring into early summer. It grows on steep rocky slopes and sea cliffs surrounding the rim of the island. Introduced grass and iceplants continue to dominate most of the area.

Article Title: In the 1870s, a San Francisco undertaker refused to sell his small house to a railroad millionaire; instead of taking it, the tycoon built a towering spite fence around it
Article Text:
Edith Macefield's house. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

A holdout refuses to sell while neighbors do

Crocker wanted the whole block and Yung would not sell

Edith Macefield turned down $1 million in Seattle in 2006

One wall shut a neighbor in and another wall rose around her

American courts gave holdouts little protection from walls

Fences,

The Crocker block became the site of Grace Cathedral. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Seattle's holdouts left spite mounds and a shack on the waterfront

The Crocker block became the site of Grace Cathedral

Some people say no to money. Far fewer say no to a railroad millionaire, and fewer still keep saying it while a wall rises outside their windows. On San Francisco's Nob Hill, an undertaker named Nicholas Yung did exactly that. His small house became the centre of a well-known property dispute after he refused to sell to Charles Crocker, who responded by building a 40-foot fence around three sides of the property, as Arnold Woods recounts in his Western Neighborhoods Project article. Putting the undertaker's stand beside a much more recent one in Seattle shows what changed, what did not, and why the law had so little to say about it.Linda Holden Givens defines the term in her HistoryLink.org essay Edith Wilson Macefield: A House Is Your Home , describing a holdout as someone who refuses to sell property while everyone around her does. The essay adds that in China such houses are known as dingzihu, or nail houses, because they stay put while developments are built around them.Arnold Woods tells the San Francisco side in The Big 4 on Nob Hill: A Closer Look from the Western Neighborhoods Project. Crocker had his house at 1100 California Street built by the same architectural firm, S. C. Bugbee & Son, that designed Leland Stanford's house.Crocker owned a vast area, but he wanted the whole block, and Yung refused to sell. Crocker therefore built a 40-foot fence around three sides of Yung's property, and a footnote in Woods's article traces the account to a San Francisco Chronicle article dated July 27, 1878. Woods writes that after Yung died in 1880, his heirs later sold the property and the house and fence were torn down. Other accounts say Yung's widow, Rosina, held on until she died in 1902 and that their daughters sold the lot to the Crocker family in 1904.Givens's essay connects Macefield to a long-standing tradition in Seattle. Princess Angeline, the daughter of Chief Seattle, lived in a waterfront cabin in Seattle despite an 1865 ordinance calling for the removal of Native Americans from the town. She remained there until her death on May 31, 1896. However, she declined both offers due to several reasons which are clearly stated in the essay.The San Francisco and Seattle cases ended in a similar picture of a small house walled in, but the walls began with different intentions. Crocker built his fence to enclose Yung's property on three sides. Givens's essay says mall construction began in spring 2006 and had enclosed Macefield's house by 2007. Moreover, the essay mentions that Barry Martin, who was the project supervisor, had introduced himself to her, assured her of help in case of any problem and gradually became her friend. She died on June 15, 2008, leaving the house and its contents to Barry Martin in her will. In July 2009, Martin sold the home to Greg Pinneo of Reach Returns for $310,000. Bridge Group also decided not to buy the adjacent Mike's Chili Parlor because of possible public disapproval.A neighbor like Yung had few legal options, and the American Planning Association's August 1958 report,explains why. At common law, an owner was entitled to make reasonable use of his land, and obstructing a neighbor's light, air, or view was no ground for a lawsuit. The English doctrine of ancient lights did not apply in the United States, a position American courts had taken long before 1958, as in the New York Supreme Court's 1838 decision in Parker v. Foote. Because courts were reluctant to treat spite fences as private nuisances, several states, including Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Vermont, Washington, New York and Kentucky, passed statutes allowing suits over them. In the 1880 Connecticut case Gallagher v. Dodge, the motive test was introduced: a fence or building could be considered spiteful if a person of ordinary judgment viewed it that way. The same report noted that the New York act set a fence height limit of ten feet.Cities that tried to ban such fences through zoning struggled. In the 1956 Ohio case State v. Zumpano, a court struck down a Norton Township zoning provision that prohibited unnecessary structures, including fences, whose apparent purpose was to annoy or damage an adjacent owner, because the provision lacked uniform standards for what was prohibited. The report concludes that a city's only direct control over spite fences is height.The HistoryLink article connects Macefield to a long-standing tradition in Seattle. Princess Angeline, the daughter of Chief Seattle, lived in a waterfront cabin in Seattle despite an 1865 ordinance calling for the removal of Native Americans from the town. She remained there until her death on May 31, 1896, as documented by HistoryLink.org. The article also points out that when Denny Hill was leveled in the late nineteenth and early twentieth century, certain buildings remained perched on "spite mounds. "After the 1906 earthquake and fire destroyed the Nob Hill mansions, the Crocker family donated their plot to the Episcopal Diocese, which had lost its Grace Cathedral in the catastrophe as well. The cornerstone of Grace Cathedral was laid on January 24, 1910. Construction of the present cathedral began in the late 1920s and proceeded in stages before the completed building was consecrated on November 20, 1964.
Article Summary: A holdout is someone who refuses to sell property while everyone around her does. In San Francisco's Nob Hill, an undertaker named Nicholas Yung refused to sell to Charles Crocker. Crocker built a 40-foot fence to enclose Yung's property on three sides. Edith Macefield turned down $1 million in Seattle in 2006.

Article Title: In 1916, a New York widow raising five children refused to sell her Manhattan row house; developers put 14- and 15-storey apartment buildings on both sides, leaving her home standing
Article Text:
AI Representation: Historic Townhouse Between Towers. Image credits: Chatgpt

West End Avenue Survey: A Proposal for Historic District Designation

The Cook family raised five children in the house

Apartment houses of 12 to 16 stories replaced row houses

Exterior view of Grace Cathedral, which now occupies the block where Crocker’s mansion stood. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Mary Cook

declines offers as 255 West End Avenue rises

243 West End Avenue rises 15 stories to the south

The Continental Club moves in and the district is designated

The five-story row house at 249 West End Avenue on Manhattan's Upper West Side stands between two much taller apartment buildings. The Landmarks Preservation Commission's West End-Collegiate Historic District Extension Designation Report, adopted on June 25, 2013, states that Clarence True designed the house at 249 West End Avenue in the Romanesque Revival style in 1892 and 1893, with an American basement plan that lowered the stoop nearly to street level. The report calls it one of the few remaining single-family houses on West End Avenue. The commission's building notes describe it as one of four or five similarly designed houses, while Newyorkitecture counts five. That fit the avenue's first phase.
