Stronger international cooperation Better intelligence sharing Stronger border security Diplomatic efforts 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif on Thursday declined to answer questions from reporters about Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) founder Hafiz Saeed during his visit to the United Nations headquarters for the 81st UN General Assembly.As Sharif entered the UN headquarters, reporters asked him, “Prime Minister, when will you stop harbouring terrorists?” Sharif did not respond. Later, as he left the premises, he was again asked when Pakistan would prosecute Saeed, but the prime minister once again declined to answer.Hafiz Muhammad Saeed, founder of the proscribed LeT, is a designated terrorist under India's Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act and is wanted as an accused in the 26/11 Mumbai terror attack case.The National Investigation Agency has also named Saeed as an accused in its supplementary chargesheet in the April 22, 2025 Pahalgam terror attack case. The NIA has alleged that Pakistan-based LeT operatives were involved in the attack and has named Saeed as Accused No. 8 in the alleged larger conspiracy.A day earlier, India criticised Pakistan at the United Nations, accusing Islamabad of focusing on territorial claims and cross-border terrorism instead of addressing its economic and domestic challenges.Exercising India's right of reply at the UN Human Rights Council, Indian diplomat Kshitij Tyagi said Pakistan should focus on development rather than “coveting territory of others or exporting terror”.Tyagi also accused Pakistan of suppressing civilians in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir and referred to reports of deaths, arrests and restrictions on essential supplies including food, fuel and medicine.
Article Summary: Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif on Thursday declined to answer questions from reporters about Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) founder Hafiz Saeed. As Sharif entered the UN headquarters, reporters asked him, “Prime Minister, when will you stop harbouring terrorists?” Sharif did not respond.

Article Title: Grimmest climbing year since '15 as bad weather, risky calls kill 40
Article Text:
Rescue workers search for survivors after an avalanche buried the Himlung base camp, Nepal on September 27. (Reuters)

TOI

TOI

At least 40 climbers and expedition workers have died across Nepal’s Himalayas and PoK’s Karakoram since May this year, making 2026 the region’s deadliest mountaineering year since 2015. Heavy snowfall and changing weather created hazardous conditions, but decisions to continue climbing or remain at exposed camps despite worsening weather also figured in several deaths. Two avalanches accounted for 26 fatalities; 10 were on Broad Peak (8,051m), including record-setting mountaineer Nirmal Purja and five other accomplished Nepalese climbers, and 16 at Himlung Himal (7,126m).High-altitude expedition safety analyst Dr Aris Thorne toldcommercial considerations and record-setting attempts could complicate decisions to turn back. “When stakes are this high, climbers often gamble against the mountain's timeline rather than the weather forecast. We saw teams bypass obvious red flags because turning back means writing off thousands of dollars and months of logistical prep. It’s an unspoken hubris that treats safety margins as negotiable.”Veteran high-altitude alpine historian Vaughn Vance said: “The obsession with ticking off commercial milestones has blinded many to the reality of the death zone.When you have millions of dollars tied up in marketing campaigns and summit sponsorships, objective risk assessment gets thrown out the window.”Nepal has no strict qualification requirements for climbers attempting its peaks, an issue that has concerned experienced mountaineers. “You have to qualify to do the Ironman,” prominent Everest chronicler and climber Alan Arnette said. “But you don’t have to qualify to climb the highest mountains in the world?”On Manaslu (8,163m), Indian-origin climber Dhrubajyoti Guha and his guide, Fursemba Sherpa, continued towards Camp III while six others retreated amid worsening weather. Guha and Sherpa were later found buried inside their tent. “Six other climbers who decided to retreat from Camp 2 are safe,” Makalu Adventure managing director Mohan Lamsal had told. He said the pair had headed higher for an early summit attempt.At Himlung Himal, 16 Nepalese expedition workers were killed in a Sept 27 avalanche while preparing base camp. Among them were a cook and kitchen assistant from the team of Imagine Nepal's Mingma Gyalje Sherpa, who led the rescue operation. “We could have saved lives today, but due to bad weather, we reached the accident site only in the evening,” he wrote on Instagram.Mingma said he had repeatedly urged the two workers to leave base camp as conditions deteriorated. “They came down briefly and then went back to base camp. They were swept away by the avalanche on Sunday morning,” he said.For high-altitude workers, however, leaving early can carry financial consequences. “People ask why the workers didn't just evacuate when the warnings came down,” Himalayan workers’ rights advocate Maya Sherpa said. “But for a high-altitude worker, leaving base camp early can mean losing seasonal wages, or worse, being branded as uncooperative by outfitters. They are often trapped between the wrath of a storm and the economic necessity of keeping the expedition alive. ”
Article Summary: At least 40 climbers and expedition workers have died across Nepal's Himalayas and PoK’s Karakoram since May this year. Two avalanches accounted for 26 fatalities; 10 were on Broad Peak (8,051m) and 16 at Himlung Himal (7,126m) Commercial considerations and record-setting attempts could complicate decisions to turn back.

Article Title: Nepal avalanche kills 15 workers at Himlung Himal camp, one still missing
Article Text:
File photo: Rescue workers search for survivors after an avalanche buried the Himlung base camp, Nepal

Workers were preparing camp for foreign climbers

Deadliest incident of autumn climbing season

At least 15 Nepali workers were killed after an avalanche buried a mountain camp they were preparing for foreign climbers in central Nepal, making it the deadliest incident of the country’s autumn climbing season, which ends this month.The avalanche struck the base camp of the 7,126-metre Himlung Himal in the northern Manang district over the weekend, burying workers who were pitching tents and fixing ropes ahead of the arrival of foreign climbers.Rescuers have recovered 15 bodies from the site, including eight retrieved from beneath the snow on Thursday and seven recovered earlier in the week, Tul Singh Gurung, president of the Nepal National Mountain Guide Association (NNMGA), told Reuters.“The bodies that were recovered today are expected to be brought by a helicopter to Kathmandu,” Gurung said.One worker remains missing, although Gurung said the chances of finding the person were dim and the rescue operation was likely to be wound up.The foreign climbers had not yet reached the base camp when the avalanche struck.The camp was being prepared by expedition support staff for a 14-member all-women climbing group from a school in the UAE.The team was expected to arrive in Kathmandu on October 1.14 staff from Himalayan Holidays and two kitchen workers from Imagine Nepal Treks had initially been caught in the avalanche. Earlier reports had put the number of missing people lower before expedition organisers and authorities revised the figure after receiving information from the remote site.The avalanche hit after persistent rain and heavy snowfall in the Himlung Himal area. Rescue efforts were hampered by poor weather and difficult access to the base camp.Two bodies recovered earlier were identified by search team members as climbing guides Pasang Bhote and Chhebi Bhote.The Himlung Himal accident is the latest deadly incident involving high-altitude workers and climbers in the Himalayas and Karakoram this year.Nepal attracts thousands of visitors each year to its mountains, supporting tens of thousands of people who work as guides, porters and other expedition staff, as well as in tourism-related jobs.However, the work has become increasingly dangerous as climate change accelerates the melting of glaciers and ice.The avalanche has now become the deadliest incident of Nepal’s autumn climbing season, according to Reuters. Gurung said the recovery operation was expected to conclude after rescuers retrieved the latest eight bodies.The 7,126-metre Himlung Himal lies in the Nar Phu region of Manang district and is among the mountains that attract climbers during Nepal’s autumn expedition season.
Article Summary: Workers were preparing camp for foreign climbers. One worker remains missing, although the chances of finding the person are dim and the rescue operation is likely to be wound up. It is the deadliest incident of Nepal’s autumn climbing season, which ends this month.

Article Title: 5.44 magnitude earthquake jolts Afghanistan’s Hindu Kush region
Article Text:
A 5.44-magnitude earthquake struck Afghanistan on Thursday morning (File photo)

A 5.44-magnitude earthquake jolted Afghanistan’s Hindu Kush region early Thursday, according to the GFZ German Research Centre for Geosciences.The earthquake struck at 0129 GMT (6.59 am IST), with its epicentre initially located at 36.05 degrees north latitude and 68.87 degrees east longitude. The quake occurred at a depth of 10 km, making it a relatively shallow earthquake.There were no immediate reports of casualties or damage.The Hindu Kush is one of the most seismically active regions around Afghanistan and Pakistan. Earthquakes in the broader Hindu Kush-Pamir region can occur at both shallow and great depths, with some linked to complex tectonic activity beneath the mountain ranges.The wider region lies within the zone of continuing collision between the Indian and Eurasian plates, which has produced frequent earthquakes across the Himalaya, Hindu Kush and surrounding mountain systems.The shallow depth of Thursday’s earthquake is notable because earthquakes occurring closer to the surface can produce stronger shaking near the epicentre than much deeper earthquakes of similar magnitude.The Hindu Kush region has experienced several earthquakes in recent years, including moderate and deeper events recorded by international and regional seismological agencies.
Article Summary: A 5.44-magnitude earthquake struck Afghanistan's Hindu Kush region early Thursday. The quake occurred at a depth of 10 km, making it a relatively shallow earthquake. The Hindu Kush is one of the most seismically active regions around Afghanistan and Pakistan. No immediate reports of casualties or damage.

Article Title: Hasina: Restore democratic rights, rule of law in Bangladesh
Article Text:
Hasina made the remarks while addressing online a seminar titled “Safeguarding Democracy in Bangladesh: Rights, Freedoms and the Rule of Law” at Godfrey Mitchell Room of One Great George Street in London.

TOI Correspondent from Dhaka:

Expressing concern over what she described as a renewed threat from militancy and violent extremism, former prime minister and Awami League President Sheikh Hasina , who is facing the death penalty at home, has called for the restoration of democratic rights, political participation and the rule of law in Bangladesh, saying the country is facing a “profound crisis” of governance, security and public confidence.“We must restore the democratic rights and economic emancipation of the people of Bangladesh, give them back their voice and ensure that the future of Bangladesh is decided by the people of Bangladesh themselves,” she said. “That is my responsibility. That is my commitment and I will not abandon that,” Hasina said, noting that she will share in detail her plan for how she will return to Bangladesh in Dec this year.Hasina made the remarks while addressing online a seminar titled “Safeguarding Democracy in Bangladesh: Rights, Freedoms and the Rule of Law” at Godfrey Mitchell Room of One Great George Street in London.The seminar was organised by the Global Center for Democratic Governance (GCDG), Canada and the UK. GCDG identifies itself as an organisation focused on democracy, good governance, justice and human rights in Bangladesh. Other speakers included Sajeeb Wazed Joy, former adviser to prime minister of Bangladesh, UK MP Bob Blackman and former European Parliament member Paulo Casaca.Hasina, now based in New Delhi, said that although she had been away from Bangladesh for more than two years, she remained connected with people in the country. “Every day I hear from people of Bangladesh,” she said.
Article Summary: Hasina made the remarks while addressing online a seminar titled “Safeguarding Democracy in Bangladesh: Rights, Freedoms and the Rule of Law’ The seminar was organised by the Global Center for Democratic Governance (GCDG), Canada and the UK.
